# Getting started

*Written against `v0.11.0`. The transcripts below are generated by this site's CI, which builds the `burroughs` CLI
at the latest release tag and runs each session in `examples/cli/`. Blocks labelled as fragments are not run by it.*

## Requirements

- **Go 1.26 or newer.** The module's `go.mod` says `go 1.26`, which is the language floor. It also carries
  `toolchain go1.26.9`. That line only applies when you build *inside* the Burroughs repository, where its Makefile
  pins it exactly. As a dependency of your module, your own toolchain is used.
- **No cgo, no C toolchain.** The engine imports only the Go standard library.
- **64-bit Linux or macOS.** These are what CI tests. Windows runs the tests in a separate CI workflow that is measured, not a gate, so treat it
  as unsupported.

## Add it to a module

``` { .console .fragment }
$ go mod init example.com/fetch
$ go get github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs@v0.11.0
go: downloading github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs v0.11.0
go: added github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs v0.11.0
```

The package is `burroughs`, imported as `github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs`. Everything public is in that one package.
Everything under `internal/` is engine and not API.

## Get the CLI

Build a binary, or run it without installing:

``` { .console .fragment }
$ go install github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs/cmd/burroughs@v0.11.0
$ go run github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs/cmd/burroughs@v0.11.0 version
```

Either way, `burroughs version` prints:

```console title="examples/cli/transcripts/gs-version.txt"
--8<-- "examples/cli/transcripts/gs-version.txt"
```

!!! bug "Known issue: the banner says `v0.0.1` ([#1130](https://github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs/issues/1130))"
    The `version` banner is a fixed string in `cmd/burroughs/main.go`, not the module version, so it has said
    `v0.0.1` at every release so far, including `v0.11.0`. To find out which version you have, look at your
    `go.mod` or run `go version -m $(which burroughs)`.

## Your first module

Save this as `calc.wat`:

```wat title="examples/embed-core/calc.wat"
--8<-- "examples/embed-core/calc.wat"
```

Burroughs reads **binary** modules (`.wasm`) only. The engine contains a WAT parser, but it is internal and neither
the CLI nor the API exposes it. Assemble with any WAT assembler. These docs used `wasm-tools` 1.258.0:

``` { .console .fragment }
$ wasm-tools parse calc.wat -o calc.wasm
```

(This site's `examples/embed-core/calc.wasm` is that output, committed. The engine repository also ships `examples/add/add.wasm`, already assembled, if you want to skip this step.)

List the exports, then call some. In these transcripts, `[exit N]` is the CLI's exit status when it is not 0:

```console title="examples/cli/transcripts/gs-calc.txt"
--8<-- "examples/cli/transcripts/gs-calc.txt"
```

Arguments are **typed**: `i32:42`, not `42`. The last command shows an untyped value being refused.

A result is printed in the same spelling an argument takes, so you can feed one back in as the other.

## The same thing from Go

``` { .go .fragment }
wasm, err := os.ReadFile("calc.wasm")
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
in, err := burroughs.Instantiate(wasm)
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
res, err := in.Call("add", burroughs.I32(2), burroughs.I32(40))
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(res[0].Int32()) // 42
```

[Tutorial 1](tutorials/01-call-an-export.md) builds this out into a complete program. The [embedding
guide](embedding.md) covers the whole API.

## What `burroughs run` does with a file

`run` looks at the file and picks one of three paths. You do not choose the path:

1. A **WASI preview 1 command** (it imports `wasi_snapshot_preview1` and exports `_start`) runs as a program. Its
   arguments go after `--`, and its exit code becomes the CLI's.
2. A **component** runs its `wasi:cli/run` export. (Known issue, to be fixed in `v0.12.0`: with guest arguments,
   `--dir` or `--features`, a component is misrouted and refused as malformed;
   see [#1128](https://github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs/issues/1128) and the
   [CLI reference](cli.md#what-does-not-work-for-components-through-the-cli-v0110).)
3. Anything else is a **core module**. It is instantiated, and then either its exports are listed or the function
   you name is called.

The [CLI reference](cli.md) has every flag and exit code.
